title: Stable Dependencies Principle Violation (SDP)
pattern: A component with a high number of incoming dependencies (a highly stable, hard-to-change component) depends directly on a component with many outgoing dependencies (a volatile, rapidly changing component).
why_bad: It makes the stable component volatile or freezes the volatile component. Because many things depend on `CoreCalculator`, you cannot easily modify `experimental_logger` without breaking the world.
detection: Static analysis calculating dependency instability indices ($I = Efferent / (Afferent + Efferent)$) showing stable components depending on components with higher instability metrics.
counterexample: System-level standard libraries (like `std::*`) that are extremely stable yet accessed by everything.
fix:
Invert the dependency. Let the stable component define a clean interface (trait) it requires, and let the volatile component implement that interface.
```rust
trait Logger { fn log(&self, msg: &str); } // Declared in stable core
```
source: Robert C. Martin, *Clean Architecture* (2017), Chapter 14 ("SDP: The Stable Dependencies Principle").
